latest_daily.title: Small teams, big fights, and why AI spend compounds: two operators name what the numbers show
latest_daily.summary: Two cards, no new operators. Ethan Mollick's November 24 thread surfaces a pattern at large enterprises: 2-3 person AI-equipped teams doing the work of dozens, with management fights and no playbook to handle them. Tom Tunguz's November 24 essay quantifies the demand side of AI pricing: elasticity of 4.3-6.8x on the Ramp and OpenRouter panels means AI spend is compounding like copper, not deflating like lightbulbs.

recent_daily.title: Reputation earned, gaps AI didn't close, and the attention cost of teaching taste
recent_daily.summary: Three cards. Lily Ray's November 20 SEJ essay documents where AI search actually sources trust: YouTube, Reddit, and individual LinkedIn voices dominate, while self-description gets cited but excluded. Aleyda Solis's Tech SEO Connect deck confirms AI sped up analysis without touching the 28% implementation rate. Dan Shipper's formula frames why teaching AI your taste fails unless the feedback loop pays you back in the same exchange.

recent_daily.title: Where evals break and what compounds: grader failures, reliability gaps, and the factory step teams skip
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, one new operator. Eugene Yan's analysis of twelve public LLM benchmarks surfaces three structural failure modes in how evals are built and measured. Tom Tunguz names the fourth part of an AI software factory, the curator loop, as the step that makes compounding possible. Both sources were published November 22, 2026.

recent_daily.title: Measuring what changes, not what inflates: AI metrics, model inflection points, and the judgment gap
recent_daily.summary: Five cards, no new operators. Kevin Indig on why raw AI citation counts mislead and share is the meaningful measure. Simon Willison naming the second LLM inflection point: Fable-class models that build their own tools. Ethan Mollick on the self-evaluation gap at the frontier. Dan Shipper on why judgment stays scarce when generation becomes cheap. Chris Zukowski on what makes a game structurally resistant to cloning.

recent_daily.title: Real-people footprints in AI search, and two ways AI adoption predictions get the measurement wrong
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, no new operators. Lily Ray on fresh November 2026 citation data showing YouTube, Reddit, and individual LinkedIn profiles dominate AI search, with a 23-year argument that only real people with verifiable records survive each wave of algorithmic change. Benedict Evans on two distinct failure modes in enterprise AI: mistaking tool diffusion for structural transformation, and incumbents losing the switching friction that sustained their lazy revenue.

recent_daily.title: Goal-driven agent architecture, knowledge factory curation loops, and AI product fraud economics
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, no new operators. Harrison Chase on the six architectural properties that separate goal-based agents from task-based ones. Harrison Chase on a closed curator loop for keeping production agent knowledge fresh. Claire Vo on how AI product fraud attacks inference budget rather than credentials, and the spend-rate controls that stop it.

recent_daily.title: Trillion-dollar valuation mechanics, AI data consolidation, and browser-side Python apps
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, no new operators. Tom Tunguz on how public markets cap revenue multiples once a company crosses $1T enterprise value. Tom Tunguz on the unified columnar format replacing separate AI data stores. Simon Willison on routing all browser requests through a service worker to run a full Python app client-side.

recent_daily.title: Agent clones vs. living projects, and two measurement gaps in AI search attribution
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, one new operator. Daniel Stenberg on why an AI-generated code clone accumulates no maintenance. Kevin Indig's Q4 2026 AI search meta-analysis yields two new measurement findings: a third of AI search citations appear only in fan-out sub-queries that standard monitoring tools never see, and more than 6 in 10 AI search domain appearances name no brand at all.

recent_daily.title: External sandbox architecture, harness over model, neocloud financing risk, and testing before parity
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, no new operators. Simon Willison on inverted-trust sandbox architecture for coding agents. Hamel Husain on the engineering harness as the real quality variable in production AI. Tom Tunguz on how NVIDIA's neocloud financing decisions affect customer-base diversification. Aleyda Solis on the capacity-displacement error of treating unproven AI-era signals at parity with proven technical fixes.

recent_daily.title: Buying before building, comprehension as prerequisite, and spec-writing as the last human hold
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, one new operator. Mihail Eric, teaching Stanford's CS146S and leading AI at Monaco, names three engineering principles for AI-native development: buy tools to learn before you build, maintain comprehension as the prerequisite for reliable agent delegation, and treat spec-writing and code review as the two irreducible human choke points in a fully automated codebase.

recent_daily.title: Agent safety architecture, the attention bottleneck, and decision models in code
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, no new operators. Simon Willison publishes the external sandbox pattern, which makes coding agent safety independent of model judgment. Dan Shipper names human attention as the new bottleneck in AI feedback loops. Swyx documents System One decision models as the structured alternative to unreliable LLM chains.

recent_daily.title: Pricing tiers, slop asymmetry, and factory pressure
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, no new operators. Tom Tunguz runs Databricks production data showing the enterprise AI market has split: Anthropic at 94% of frontier-tier token volume (quality-led) and OpenAI at 81% of low-end (price-led, 90% cuts). The No AI Slop Manifesto from the AIE Code Summit names the structural reason slop compounds. Dex Horthy at the same summit completes the picture: speeding only the builder side stalls delivery because the verification side doesn't scale with it.

recent_daily.title: Agent economics and the human remainder
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, no new operators. Tom Tunguz maps why retailers block AI shopping agents (upsells are where profit lives, not base products). Georgi Gerganov ships llama.cpp v1.0.0 and semantic versioning moves local AI inference to buildable infrastructure. Tunguz and Thorsten Ball converge, from different angles, on what stays human when AI clears the operational floor.

recent_daily.title: Job descriptions have already changed
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, one new operator. Lenny Rachitsky's late-2026 job market survey finds AI fluency has displaced SQL and Python as the top PM skill, while design hiring has collapsed to record lows. On the engineering side, Swaminathan Sivasubramanian documents AWS producing 200-service infrastructure with no human code authorship and names what that means for quality: the engineer's job is now the pipeline, not the code.

recent_daily.title: What stays human when generation is cheap
recent_daily.summary: Five cards, four new operators. Dan Shipper delivers the mechanism at the center of Every's annual thesis conference: generation is now cheap, so ranking and perspective become the scarce skills. Four operators attending the same conference converge on adjacent answers about what that means for work, hiring, product design, and creative expression.

recent_daily.title: AI value chain economics and the two optimization myths
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, three operators. Tom Tunguz publishes two back-to-back posts mapping where AI gross profit actually lives and what Jensen Huang's resignation means for AI capital flows. Kevin Indig and Antoine van der Lee independently surface the same pattern: a common optimization assumption that measurement disproves.

recent_daily.title: Proxy failures, measurement gaps, and the limits of learning from a distance
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, four operators. Ethan Mollick and Aleyda Solis publish from different domains on the same underlying problem: measuring the wrong thing. Thorsten Ball and Chris Zukowski converge on a separate idea that only direct experience reveals true capability, in AI coding and in games.

recent_daily.title: AI economics at two scales, and scope discipline in generated systems
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, two operators. Simon Willison and Tom Tunguz publish from independent angles on how to measure AI costs correctly, where US token supply runs out, and what distinguishes companies that bend trajectories from companies that only move faster. Willison adds a design constraint for LLM-generated data apps.

recent_daily.title: Agents expanding their reach, and the judgment gap they still cannot close
recent_daily.summary: Four cards. Simon Willison (Nov 9) on keeping human editorial judgment visible in AI-generated PR descriptions. Simon Willison (Nov 9) on giving coding agents a sensory channel through browser APIs. Ethan Mollick (Nov 9) on self-evaluation as the new jagged frontier gap. Thorsten Ball (Nov 8) on the SDLC boundary agents can own up to but not past.

recent_daily.title: Judgment as scarce resource, and the library function as bottleneck
recent_daily.summary: Two cards. Ann Handley (Exit Five Podcast #409, Oct 29) on the marketing shift from speed to judgment when AI makes output cheap. Simon Willison (Nov 8) on how a narrow hand-tuned parser outperforms a standard library function regardless of language.

recent_daily.title: Performance-based creator pay, the SEO execution gap, and zero-click visitor pre-qualification
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, one new operator. Hector Serrano (Wispr Flow) on paying UGC creators a share of ad spend as a quality filter. Aleyda Solis on why only 28% of SEO teams implement 80%+ of their own recommendations. Rand Fishkin on conversion rates rising as traffic falls when platforms pre-qualify visitors.

recent_daily.title: Power limits AI scale, $90 opens company networks, and LLM alignment verification is fundamentally broken
recent_daily.summary: Three cards, no new operators. Tom Tunguz's November 4 post yields one card on electrical power as the binding ceiling on 2027 AI compute. His November 6 post yields one card on how AI-agent attacks collapsed enterprise intrusion costs 99% in five months. Sean Goedecke's November 2 post yields one card arguing that knowing whether an LLM is reliably aligned is impossible in principle.

recent_daily.title: Engineers become AI team leads, and proxy metrics capture the wrong audience
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, two new operators. Bart Butler's Proton engineering manifesto yields one card on the engineer's role shift from code writer to AI team leader. Simon Willison's November 3 experiment yields one card on local 27B models interpreting neural network weights. Sean Goedecke yields two cards: one on engagement metrics driving away thoughtful readers, one on noticing as the scarce AI delegation skill.

recent_daily.title: AI search displacement forces platform pivots, and verification economics govern model choice
recent_daily.summary: Four cards, three operators. Eric Seufert's analysis of Reddit's Q3 2026 earnings and Apple's App Store slowdown yields two cards on how AI search displacement changes platform monetization strategy. Simon Willison's llm 0.37 release notes yield one card on absorbing AI-assisted PR floods in open source. Thorsten Ball's October 25 essay yields one card on the false economy of cheaper models when error rate requires universal verification.

recent_daily.title: AI lab margin mechanics, channel portfolio under search decline, and trust signal erosion
recent_daily.summary: Four cards from four operators. Tom Tunguz's November 3 essay on Anthropic's S-1 yields one card on the GPU duration mismatch that will define AI lab margins in 2027. Kevin Indig's November 2 Growth Memo yields one card on email as a floor channel when organic search falls. Ethan Mollick's November Wharton piece yields one card on the verification-cost trap in Conjurer-mode delegation. Kyle Kingsbury's October 31 Jepsen analysis yields one card on LLM-generated docs eroding documentation as a trust signal.

recent_daily.title: AI stack economics from four angles, and a broken measurement baseline
recent_daily.summary: Four cards from two operators. Tom Tunguz's November 2 essay on the four questions of AI yields three cards on stack economics: harness-layer margin mechanics, thin-wrapper mortality, and the double-pendulum coupling across all four layers. Simon Willison's November 2 post on the Census Bureau's survey wording changes yields one card on how the headline AI adoption data broke.

recent_daily.title: Training weight resistance, two context failure modes, and the hyperscaler funding race
recent_daily.summary: Three cards from two operators. Drew Breunig's October 24 essay on context engineering yields two more uncaptured failure modes: training-era priors that resist runtime instructions, and a hallucinated fact embedding itself as an unresolvable goal constraint. Tom Tunguz's October 29 analysis of Q3 hyperscaler earnings maps the race between building a trillion-dollar AI compute business and the yield compression in the legacy cash flows that fund it.

recent_daily.title: Agent workflow discipline and AI peer review outperforming human experts
recent_daily.summary: Five cards from two operators. Thorsten Ball published a 15-point guide to working with coding agents on October 25; four cards pull the most distinct mechanisms. Gary King and Steven Worthington published a Harvard controlled study on October 28 showing Claude Opus 4.8 outperformed paid human expert reviewers on every measured review dimension across 124 papers.

recent_daily.title: Context distraction, AI-vs-Google behavioral divergence, and the branding channel reframe
recent_daily.summary: Four cards from three operators. Drew Breunig names a fifth context failure mode: contradictory examples in chat history override explicit instructions, backed by a 13-model experiment. Cate Dombrowski at iPullRank matches 16,310 users across Google and AI panels and finds 96% of AI prompts have no Google counterpart in the same session. Mike King argues that judging AI search by referral traffic is a category error because AI answers are earned media composed by machines, not click competitors.

recent_daily.title: AI game design taste, answer-first AEO, clone defense, AI economics, and the hourly deploy loop
recent_daily.summary: Five cards from five operators. Simon Willison calls October 2026 the inflection point for vibe coding games, now that models can produce fun gameplay rather than just working code. Mike Taylor runs 2,484-session experiments showing that agents cite answer-first headlines and ignore curiosity framing. Chris Zukowski documents the first AI clone overtaking an original game on Steam, and maps the three conditions that make it happen. Tom Tunguz measures AI application revenue catching up to infrastructure spend twice as fast as the web era did, with a circularity warning. Jacob Sansbury describes Spawn, a game studio where an hour without a production deploy is a SEV-0.
